title: Longest Valid Parentheses
statement:
A string made of the characters `'('` and `')'` is valid when it is the empty string, or when it can be split into two valid strings, or when it is a valid string wrapped in a matching pair. Equivalently, a bracket string is valid when every prefix has at least as many `'('` as `')'` and the whole string has equally many of each.

Given the bracket string `s`, where every character is either `'('` or `')'`, return the length of the longest contiguous slice of `s` that is a valid bracket string. A slice is a run of consecutive characters; a valid slice must be non-empty to count. Return 0 when no non-empty valid slice exists.

For example, in `"(()"` the longest valid slice is `"()"` with length 2, in `")()())"` it is `"()()"` with length 4, and in `"("` there is none, so the answer is 0.

Constraints: `1 <= s.length <= 200` and every character of `s` is `'('` or `')'`.

constraints: Inputs are JSON-serializable values satisfying the bounds stated above.
hints: Do not try to count pairs. For each position ask a narrower question instead: what is the longest valid slice that ends exactly here?

When the current character is `')'`, the previous character decides the case. If it is `'('` you have a pair plus whatever valid slice ended before it. If it is `')'`, its own slice has a known length, and the character just left of that slice must be `'('` to close it; the slice before that opener can then be glued on as well.
The answer is the maximum over every ending position, because a trailing unmatched bracket means the best slice does not end at the last index.

editorial.approach: The brute force fixes a starting index and sweeps right keeping a running balance of `'('` minus `')'`. A slice is valid exactly when the balance never drops below zero and comes back to zero, so each zero hit is a candidate answer; once the balance goes negative the start index is dead and the inner loop breaks. That is O(n^2). The optimal version keeps a one-dimensional table where `dp[i]` is the length of the longest valid slice ending at index `i`. A `')'` at `i` either pairs with a `'('` at `i - 1`, giving 2 plus `dp[i - 2]`, or closes a block that already ends at `i - 1`: that block has length `dp[i - 1]`, the character immediately to its left must be `'('`, and when it is, the new length is `dp[i - 1] + 2` plus the valid slice ending just before that opener.
editorial.why_optimal: The whole string must be read, and every DP entry is filled by looking back at a constant number of positions, so O(n) time is the floor; the table costs O(n) space and carries the recurrence directly. A monotonic stack reaches the same O(n) time bound, so no approach beats linear here. With n at most 200 the O(n^2) brute force is still instant and serves as the cross-check.
editorial.pitfalls: Returning `dp[n - 1]` instead of the maximum over all positions, which fails on `")()"` and on any string whose last character leaves a slice open. Off-by-one in the jump `i - dp[i - 1] - 1`, which must land exactly on the character that closes the inner block. Forgetting to add the slice ending before that opener, which under-counts strings such as `"()(())"`. All `'('` or all `')'` input must return 0, and a single character must never be reported as valid.
